reason: Both are accurate (5 of 14 for the prefix gate, 0 of 14 for the scoped gates, read only 4 of 8, scoped and approval bound indistinguishable, ceiling-by-design caveat), and A's fixed dark chalkboard stage with an animated folder map is the more GIF-ready of the two. B teaches better for a non-engineer. In its step 3, each of the five tricks is its own guess with 'Right' or 'Not quite' feedback, a plain-language reason and a step-by-step walk of the path. Trick 4 there explains why order matters (enter the link, then go up, so you land in /srv/private.txt and not where text tidying says). A packs four tricks into one auto-cycling step 4 with a single sentence, never explains the link-then-parent order, and its step 3 guess feedback does not tell a wrong guesser they were wrong. B's gate tester shows the reasoning of each gate ('Is that inside /workspace/acme/tmp/? No'). Its scoreboard lets you tap any of the 110 squares to see the actual request, and its last screen frames 5 of 14 as 'a list of tricks it misses, not a failure rate'. That makes B the more Khan-style lesson, although its long scrolling views make it harder to turn into a GIF.

A: Step 4 auto-cycles four different tricks in one step with one sentence of explanation. The link-then-parent case (ends at /srv/private.txt, while text tidying says tmp/private.txt) is never explained, and in the end frame I captured, the .env item had no number 4 marker.

Step 3 guess feedback is the same whatever you pick ('It lets it through...'). It never says 'not quite' to someone who guessed 'Blocks it'. The step 6 tester also treats a bare relative path like 'hello' as inside the project and allowed by the scoped gate.

Step 8 puts 'missed all 5 such tricks' under 'Follow every .. and link', but two of the five (tmp-other look-alike folder and .env secret) are not .. or link tricks. Each card also has a large empty band between the caption and the legend.
B: Views are long scrolling pages at 390 px (the scoreboard is about 1,400 px tall). The rules map, the path walk and the tapped-square detail sit below the fold, so it is weaker as a fixed-frame GIF for LinkedIn.
Step 2's 'Your turn' uses /workspace/acme/tmp-other/archive, then step 3 opens with the same path as trick 1, so the first trick is a repeat.

The trick chip row is clipped sideways at phone width. Tapping a square shows internal case IDs ('link_then_parent', 'traversal') and marks read-only's by-design blocks as '(wrong)' with no explanation next to it.
